databases_sql.notes: SQL is taught as its own language, run through sqlite3 in-memory databases (all snippets executed). Entry topic uses `import sqlite3` / `connect(':memory:')` / `execute` as a three-line template that lib_sqlite3.connect_execute_fetch explains immediately after. INTEGER PRIMARY KEY mechanics live in constraints; choosing keys and foreign keys belong to data_modeling. Indexes (CREATE INDEX), normalization theory, PostgreSQL, DB Browser for SQLite and migrations are out of scope per plan.json; a logical key's UNIQUE constraint is the only performance idea taught. CASE expressions, views, transactions beyond commit/rollback, window functions and UPSERT (ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE) were left out. manage_tables and subqueries are non-core.

lib_sqlite3.notes: Owns the Python side: connect/execute/fetch, placeholders and SQL injection (the injection_attacks concept is out of scope, so its sqlite3-relevant part lives here), commit/with/executescript, lastrowid/rowcount/IntegrityError, sqlite3.Row, and a file-loading topic (py4e counting-email pattern). Uses `import csv`/`import json` as earlier batches did. B18 pandas.read_sql could depend on connect_execute_fetch.

sql_joins.notes: inner_join is core; left_join and multi_table_joins are non-core. Self-joins, RIGHT/FULL OUTER JOIN (FULL needs SQLite 3.39+) and CROSS JOIN by name were left out; the every-combination bug covers the cross-join idea.

data_modeling.notes: py4e Chapter 15 data modeling: split_into_tables (a practical 'normalization' without normal forms), keys, get_or_create_id (py4e Tracks pattern) and many_to_many. ER diagram notation is described in text (artists 1 --< albums) rather than given a topic.

lib_sqlalchemy.notes: SQLAlchemy 2.0 declarative style (DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, select, Session) rather than the legacy Query API; Flask-SQLAlchemy (100 Days' actual tool) is its own topic. Not installed locally, so snippets were not run; outputs (echo SQL, ids) are described from the documented behaviour. Alembic migrations are out of scope (db_migrations).

web_development.notes: Server-side view only. how_web_apps_work models routing as a dict of functions (runnable without Flask) and introduces 200/404/500 from the server's side; the client side of HTTP (methods, headers, status codes, requests library) is B16 apis_http, running in parallel, and the stitching pass should link B16's request/response topic as a prerequisite of how_web_apps_work or have it encompass that KP. html_css_basics is out of scope, but Flask needs a little HTML, so html_for_python_devs teaches tags, links, forms and html.escape (XSS) only; CSS and Bootstrap are not taught. Static site generation is B20. Reconciliation: how_web_apps_work now depends on B16 apis_http.request_response_cycle (owner of HTTP requests, responses, methods and status codes); KP1 and KP3 were reframed as the server side instead of re-teaching them.

lib_flask.notes: Five non-core topics following 100 Days Days 54-62. Flask is not installed, so no snippet was run; Flask's test_client is taught in KP3 of first_app_and_routes so the platform can auto-grade views without a browser. Blueprints, the application factory, Flask's g and before_request were left out (no course teaches them). Sessions/login live in authentication; JSON APIs in rest_api_design; database access in lib_sqlalchemy.flask_sqlalchemy.

lib_jinja.notes: Three non-core topics. Only expressions_and_filters KP1 uses jinja2.Template directly; the rest are Flask templates. Macros, custom filters and whitespace control were left out.

lib_wtforms.notes: Flask-WTF + WTForms (100 Days Days 61-62). Bootstrap-Flask's render_form (Flask-Bootstrap) is lib_bootstrap, out of scope. Not installed; error texts quoted from WTForms' standard messages.

authentication.notes: Six non-core topics. Hashing, salting and pbkdf2 use hashlib/secrets from the standard library and were run; register_and_login was run end to end with sqlite3. werkzeug, Flask-Login and JWT are described, not run. Authorization (out of scope as its own concept) appears only as the admin_only decorator KP in login_sessions. api_tokens comes after rest_api_design.write_endpoints. MFA/TOTP, OAuth sign-in and password reset flows were left out.

rest_api_design.notes: Three non-core topics (100 Days Day 66). resources_and_methods carries pending concept:apis_http (B16) because it reuses HTTP methods and status codes from the client view; it re-states them only as a design table. Endpoints use sqlite3 + sqlite3.Row rather than SQLAlchemy so they need only core database topics plus Flask; the SQLAlchemy version is a practice variation. Pagination, versioning and OpenAPI were left out; API keys in DELETE are the bridge to authentication.api_tokens.

deployment.notes: Two non-core topics (100 Days Day 71). Git/GitHub, Docker, PostgreSQL administration and HTTPS are out of scope; pushing to GitHub appears as a memorised step. Builds on B13 environment_variables.secrets_out_of_code and tool_pip.requirements_files as B13 suggested.

topics.title: Databases, tables and your first SQL statements
topics.summary: Picture a table as rows and columns, create one with CREATE TABLE, add a row with INSERT and read it back with SELECT *, writing SQL inside a Python string.

knowledge_points.title: A table is rows and columns
knowledge_points.worked_example:
title  | year
Dune   | 1965
Emma   | 1815
A table has named columns; each row is one record, like the tuple ('Dune', 1965). A database file holds many tables.
knowledge_points.practice: Read a drawn table: count rows and columns, name the column holding a value, write a row as a tuple.

knowledge_points.title: Create a table with CREATE TABLE
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE books (title TEXT, year INTEGER)")
Every column gets a name and a type (TEXT, INTEGER, REAL). The first two lines are a template that the next topic explains.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the CREATE TABLE statement for a described table; choose TEXT, INTEGER or REAL for each column.

knowledge_points.title: Add a row with INSERT, read it with SELECT *
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("INSERT INTO books VALUES ('Dune', 1965)")
print(db.execute("SELECT * FROM books").fetchall())
# [('Dune', 1965)]
SELECT * means every column; the rows come back as a list of tuples.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the printed list after one or two INSERTs; write the INSERT for a given row.

knowledge_points.title: SQL inside a Python string: keywords and quotes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("insert into books values ('Emma', 1815)")  # works: keywords ignore case
db.execute("INSERT INTO books VALUES (Emma, 1815)")
# sqlite3.OperationalError: no such column: Emma
SQL text values need single quotes inside the double-quoted Python string; keywords are written in CAPITALS by convention.
knowledge_points.practice: Find and fix the quoting bug in INSERT statements; choose which statements run.

topics.title: Running SQL from Python: connect, execute and fetch
topics.summary: Open a database with sqlite3.connect, run statements with execute, and get rows back with fetchall, fetchone or a for loop.

knowledge_points.title: connect() opens a database, execute() runs one statement
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")   # a fresh database in memory
cur = db.execute("SELECT 1 + 1")
print(cur.fetchall())  # [(2,)]
":memory:" is thrown away when the program ends; a file name such as "books.db" keeps the data (see saving changes).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the result of simple SELECT expressions; choose between ':memory:' and a file name for described situations.

knowledge_points.title: fetchall() returns a list of tuples
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("CREATE TABLE books (title TEXT, year INTEGER)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO books VALUES ('Dune', 1965), ('Emma', 1815)")
print(db.execute("SELECT title FROM books").fetchall())
# [('Dune',), ('Emma',)]
Even a one-column row is a tuple, so the first title is rows[0][0].
knowledge_points.practice: Predict fetchall() results; write the indexing expression that gets one value out of the result.

knowledge_points.title: fetchone() takes one row at a time, then None
knowledge_points.worked_example:
cur = db.execute("SELECT title, year FROM books")
print(cur.fetchone())  # ('Dune', 1965)
print(cur.fetchone())  # ('Emma', 1815)
print(cur.fetchone())  # None
The cursor remembers its place; None means no rows are left.
knowledge_points.practice: Trace a sequence of fetchone/fetchall calls; fix code that indexes the result without checking for None.

knowledge_points.title: Loop over the cursor and unpack each row
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for title, year in db.execute("SELECT title, year FROM books"):
    print(title, year)
# Dune 1965
# Emma 1815
A cursor can be looped over directly, one tuple per row.
knowledge_points.practice: Write a loop that prints rows in a format; predict the output of a loop over a query.

topics.title: Choosing columns and rows: SELECT and WHERE
topics.summary: Select specific columns and filter rows with WHERE using comparisons on numbers and text, combined with AND, OR and NOT.

knowledge_points.title: Name the columns you want
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(db.execute("SELECT title FROM books").fetchall())
# [('Dune',), ('Emma',), ('Ubik',)]
(books holds Dune 1965, Emma 1815, Ubik 1969) The columns come back in the order you list them.
knowledge_points.practice: Write SELECT statements for requested columns; predict the shape of each result.

knowledge_points.title: Filter rows with WHERE and a comparison
knowledge_points.worked_example:
q = "SELECT title FROM books WHERE year > 1900"
print(db.execute(q).fetchall())  # [('Dune',), ('Ubik',)]
SQL tests equality with a single = and inequality with != (or <>).
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which rows a WHERE clause keeps; fix a query that uses == or a wrong operator.

knowledge_points.title: Compare text: exact and case-sensitive
knowledge_points.worked_example:
q = "SELECT * FROM books WHERE title = 'dune'"
print(db.execute(q).fetchall())  # []
Text comparisons with = match the exact characters, so 'dune' finds nothing.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of text comparisons; write a WHERE clause for a named title.

knowledge_points.title: Combine conditions with AND, OR and NOT
knowledge_points.worked_example:
q = "SELECT * FROM books WHERE year > 1900 AND title != 'Ubik'"
print(db.execute(q).fetchall())  # [('Dune', 1965)]
Use parentheses when mixing AND and OR, just as in Python.
knowledge_points.practice: Translate English filters into WHERE clauses; predict the rows a compound condition keeps.

topics.title: Sorting and trimming results: ORDER BY, LIMIT and DISTINCT
topics.summary: Sort query results by one or more columns in either direction, keep only the first rows, page through results and remove duplicate values.

knowledge_points.title: Sort with ORDER BY
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(db.execute("SELECT * FROM books ORDER BY title").fetchall())
# [('Dune', 1965), ('Emma', 1815), ('Ubik', 1969)]
Without ORDER BY the database may return rows in any order, so sort whenever order matters.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the order of rows for ORDER BY on a number or text column.

knowledge_points.title: Descending order and several sort keys
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT title FROM books ORDER BY author, year DESC
(books now also has an author column.) Rows are sorted by author first; rows with the same author are sorted newest first. DESC applies only to the column right before it.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the order for two-key sorts; fix a query where DESC is on the wrong column.

knowledge_points.title: Keep the first rows with LIMIT and OFFSET
knowledge_points.worked_example:
q = "SELECT * FROM books ORDER BY year DESC LIMIT 2"
print(db.execute(q).fetchall())  # [('Ubik', 1969), ('Dune', 1965)]
LIMIT 2 OFFSET 2 skips two rows first: page two of a two-per-page list.
knowledge_points.practice: Write top-n queries; compute which rows a LIMIT/OFFSET page shows.

knowledge_points.title: Remove duplicates with DISTINCT
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT DISTINCT author FROM books ORDER BY author
# [('Austen',), ('Dick',), ('Herbert',)]  (Austen wrote two of the books)
DISTINCT keeps one copy of each distinct row.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict DISTINCT results; choose between DISTINCT and a plain SELECT for a question.

topics.title: Patterns, lists and missing values: LIKE, IN, BETWEEN and NULL
topics.summary: Filter with text patterns, lists of values and ranges, and handle NULL (missing) values correctly with IS NULL.

knowledge_points.title: Match text patterns with LIKE
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT title FROM books WHERE title LIKE 'D%'    # [('Dune',)]
SELECT title FROM books WHERE title LIKE '%u%'   # Dune, Ubik, Persuasion
(books now has title, author, year, price; Persuasion by Austen has no price yet.) % matches any run of characters and _ exactly one; in SQLite LIKE ignores case for English letters.
knowledge_points.practice: Write LIKE patterns for starts-with, ends-with and contains; predict which titles match.

knowledge_points.title: Lists and ranges: IN and BETWEEN
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT title FROM books WHERE author IN ('Dick', 'Herbert')
SELECT title FROM books WHERE year BETWEEN 1800 AND 1900
BETWEEN includes both ends, like 1800 <= year <= 1900.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite chains of OR as IN; predict whether boundary values are included.

knowledge_points.title: NULL means missing and comes back as None
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("INSERT INTO books VALUES ('Persuasion', 'Austen', 1817, NULL)")
print(db.execute("SELECT price FROM books WHERE title = 'Persuasion'").fetchone())  # (None,)
NULL is SQL's 'no value'; Python receives it as None.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict how NULL values print in Python; choose NULL vs 0 vs '' for described missing data.

knowledge_points.title: = NULL never matches: use IS NULL
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT title FROM books WHERE price = NULL     # []  (always empty)
SELECT title FROM books WHERE price IS NULL    # [('Persuasion',)]
Nothing is equal to NULL, not even NULL; IS NULL and IS NOT NULL test for it.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix queries that compare with = NULL or != NULL; predict results with missing values.

topics.title: Adding rows with INSERT
topics.summary: Insert one or several rows, naming the columns, and know what happens to columns you leave out or when the value count is wrong.

knowledge_points.title: Name the columns you are filling
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("INSERT INTO books (title, year) VALUES ('Dune', 1965)")
The values match the listed columns in order, so the statement still works if columns are added to the table later.
knowledge_points.practice: Write INSERT statements with column lists; match values to columns.

knowledge_points.title: Several rows in one INSERT
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("INSERT INTO books (title, year) VALUES ('Emma', 1815), ('Ubik', 1969)")
print(db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM books").fetchone())  # (3,)
Each pair of parentheses is one row.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the table after multi-row inserts; write one INSERT for three rows.

knowledge_points.title: Columns you leave out become NULL
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("INSERT INTO books (title, author) VALUES ('Solaris', 'Lem')")
print(db.execute("SELECT * FROM books WHERE title = 'Solaris'").fetchall())
# [('Solaris', 'Lem', None, None)]
knowledge_points.practice: Predict full rows after partial inserts.

knowledge_points.title: Too few values is an error
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("INSERT INTO books VALUES ('X', 'Y')")
# sqlite3.OperationalError: table books has 4 columns but 2 values were supplied
Fix: list the columns you are filling.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix INSERT statements whose value count does not match; explain the error message.

topics.title: Changing and removing rows: UPDATE and DELETE
topics.summary: Change values with UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE, remove rows with DELETE, and avoid the classic bug of forgetting WHERE.

knowledge_points.title: UPDATE changes the rows WHERE picks
knowledge_points.worked_example:
cur = db.execute("UPDATE books SET price = 5.0 WHERE title = 'Persuasion'")
print(cur.rowcount)  # 1
cur.rowcount tells how many rows were changed.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the table and rowcount after UPDATE statements; write an UPDATE for a described change.

knowledge_points.title: Compute the new value from the old one
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("UPDATE books SET price = price * 2 WHERE author = 'Austen'")
# Emma 4.0 -> 8.0, Persuasion 5.0 -> 10.0
SET a = 1, b = 2 changes several columns at once.
knowledge_points.practice: Write UPDATEs that increase, discount or reset values; predict values after two updates in a row.

knowledge_points.title: DELETE removes whole rows
knowledge_points.worked_example:
cur = db.execute("DELETE FROM books WHERE year < 1900")
print(cur.rowcount)  # 2
print(db.execute("SELECT title FROM books").fetchall())  # [('Dune',), ('Ubik',)]
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what remains after DELETE; write a DELETE for a described set of rows.

knowledge_points.title: Forgetting WHERE changes every row
knowledge_points.worked_example:
cur = db.execute("UPDATE books SET price = 1")
print(cur.rowcount)  # 2: every book now costs 1
Run a SELECT with the same WHERE first to see exactly which rows will change.
knowledge_points.practice: Spot UPDATE/DELETE statements that hit too many rows and fix them; choose the safe order of steps.

topics.title: Rules for columns: PRIMARY KEY, NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT and CHECK
topics.summary: Declare column rules so the database rejects bad rows, read the IntegrityError it raises, and get automatic ids from INTEGER PRIMARY KEY.

knowledge_points.title: NOT NULL and DEFAULT
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("""CREATE TABLE users (
    email TEXT NOT NULL,
    name TEXT DEFAULT 'anon')""")
db.execute("INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES ('Bo')")
# sqlite3.IntegrityError: NOT NULL constraint failed: users.email
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which inserts succeed and what values left-out columns get.

knowledge_points.title: UNIQUE forbids duplicates
knowledge_points.worked_example:
email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE
inserting 'a@x.com' twice:
# sqlite3.IntegrityError: UNIQUE constraint failed: users.email
knowledge_points.practice: Choose which columns should be UNIQUE; predict which insert in a sequence fails.

knowledge_points.title: INTEGER PRIMARY KEY numbers rows for you
knowledge_points.worked_example:
CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE, ...)
INSERT INTO users (email) VALUES ('a@x.com'), ('b@x.com')
# rows get id 1 and id 2
A primary key identifies each row; it must be unique, so inserting id 1 again fails.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the ids given to new rows; fix an INSERT that supplies a duplicate id.

knowledge_points.title: CHECK enforces a condition
knowledge_points.worked_example:
age INTEGER CHECK (age >= 0)
INSERT INTO users (email, age) VALUES ('c@x.com', -1)
# sqlite3.IntegrityError: CHECK constraint failed: age >= 0
knowledge_points.practice: Write CHECK constraints for described rules; predict which rows are rejected.

topics.title: Putting Python values into SQL safely: ? placeholders
topics.summary: Pass values to SQL with ? and :name placeholders instead of f-strings, avoiding quote bugs and SQL injection, and insert many rows with executemany.

knowledge_points.title: ? marks a value; the tuple fills it
knowledge_points.worked_example:
title, year = "Dune", 1965
db.execute("INSERT INTO books VALUES (?, ?)", (title, year))
print(db.execute("SELECT * FROM books WHERE title = ?", (title,)).fetchall())
# [('Dune', 1965)]
No quotes go around ?: sqlite3 handles them.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite queries with literal values to use placeholders; fill in the values tuple.

knowledge_points.title: One value still needs a tuple: (title,)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("SELECT * FROM books WHERE title = ?", (title))
# sqlite3.ProgrammingError: Incorrect number of bindings supplied.
#   The current statement uses 1, and there are 4 supplied.
(title) is just the string 'Dune', whose 4 characters were taken as 4 values; write (title,).
knowledge_points.practice: Fix calls with a missing trailing comma; predict the error message's numbers for other strings.

knowledge_points.title: Why not f-strings: quotes and SQL injection
knowledge_points.worked_example:
name = "Ender's Game"
db.execute(f"INSERT INTO books VALUES ('{name}', 1985)")
# sqlite3.OperationalError: near "s": syntax error
evil = "x' OR '1'='1"
db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM books WHERE title = '{evil}'")   # returns EVERY row
db.execute("SELECT * FROM books WHERE title = ?", (evil,))   # [] as it should
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what an f-string query does with hostile input; fix injectable code by switching to placeholders.

knowledge_points.title: executemany and named placeholders
knowledge_points.worked_example:
rows = [("Emma", 1815), ("Ubik", 1969)]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO books VALUES (?, ?)", rows)
db.execute("SELECT title FROM books WHERE year > :y", {"y": 1900})
Placeholders stand for values only: a table or column name cannot be a ?.
knowledge_points.practice: Insert a list of tuples with executemany; convert ? placeholders to :name with a dict; spot an illegal placeholder for a table name.

topics.title: Saving changes: database files, commit and with
topics.summary: Store a database in a file, make changes permanent with commit(), use with to commit or roll back a group of changes, and run setup scripts with executescript.

knowledge_points.title: A file database survives the program
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db = sqlite3.connect("shop.db")   # creates shop.db if it does not exist
...
db.close()
The file sits next to your program; connecting again later sees the same tables.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose when data survives a restart (memory vs file); order the open-work-close steps.

knowledge_points.title: No commit, no change
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db = sqlite3.connect("shop.db")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE items (name TEXT)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO items VALUES ('pen')")
db.close()                       # closed without commit
db = sqlite3.connect("shop.db")
print(db.execute("SELECT * FROM items").fetchall())  # []
INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE are only saved by db.commit().
knowledge_points.practice: Predict what a second connection sees after code with and without commit(); add the missing commit.

knowledge_points.title: with db: commit on success, roll back on error
knowledge_points.worked_example:
try:
    with db:
        db.execute("INSERT INTO items VALUES ('cap')")
        db.execute("INSERT INTO itemz VALUES ('lid')")  # typo
except sqlite3.OperationalError as e:
    print("rolled back:", e)   # rolled back: no such table: itemz
'cap' is not saved either: the group is all or nothing. Unlike with open(), with db does not close the connection.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the table after a with block that fails half-way; choose what with db does and does not do.

knowledge_points.title: executescript runs several statements
knowledge_points.practice: Choose execute or executescript for given SQL; fix code that passes two statements to execute.

topics.title: Summarising a table: COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX
topics.summary: Compute counts, totals, averages and extremes over rows with aggregate functions, filter first with WHERE, and read the single result into Python.

knowledge_points.title: COUNT(*) and getting one number out
knowledge_points.worked_example:
n = db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM books").fetchone()[0]
print(n)  # 4
An aggregate turns many rows into one row; fetchone()[0] unwraps the single value.
knowledge_points.practice: Write COUNT queries and the Python to read the number; predict counts for small tables.

knowledge_points.title: SUM, AVG, MIN and MAX
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT SUM(price), AVG(price), MIN(year), MAX(year) FROM books
# (20.75, 6.916666666666667, 1815, 1969)
Several aggregates can share one SELECT.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute aggregate results by hand for a 4-row table; choose the right function for a question.

knowledge_points.title: COUNT(column) skips NULLs
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(price) FROM books   # (4, 3)
Persuasion's price is NULL: COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(price) counts known prices. SUM and AVG also ignore NULL.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict counts and averages on columns containing NULL.

knowledge_points.title: Filter first, then aggregate; name the result
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM books WHERE author = 'Austen'   # (2,)
WHERE picks the rows before they are counted; AS gives the result column a name.
knowledge_points.practice: Write aggregate queries over filtered rows; predict results.

topics.title: Counting per group: GROUP BY and HAVING
topics.summary: Compute an aggregate for each group of rows, sort groups by their totals, and filter groups with HAVING versus rows with WHERE.

knowledge_points.title: One result row per group
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT author, COUNT(*) FROM books GROUP BY author
# [('Austen', 2), ('Dick', 1), ('Herbert', 1)]
The same answer as counting with a dictionary in Python, done by the database.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict grouped counts and sums for a small table; write GROUP BY queries for questions.

knowledge_points.title: Sort groups by their totals
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT author, COUNT(*) AS n FROM books
GROUP BY author ORDER BY n DESC, author
The py4e 'top senders' pattern: count per email address, biggest first, then LIMIT 10.
knowledge_points.practice: Write top-n-per-group queries; predict the order of groups.

knowledge_points.title: WHERE filters rows before grouping
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT author, COUNT(*) FROM books WHERE year > 1816 GROUP BY author
# [('Austen', 1), ('Dick', 1), ('Herbert', 1)]  (Emma, 1815, was removed first)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict grouped results when WHERE removes rows first.

knowledge_points.title: HAVING filters groups after grouping
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT author, COUNT(*) FROM books GROUP BY author HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
# [('Austen', 2)]
WHERE cannot use COUNT(*); HAVING can.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose WHERE or HAVING for described filters; fix a query that puts an aggregate in WHERE.

topics.title: New ids, changed-row counts and database errors
topics.summary: Read the id of a row you just inserted, use rowcount and fetchone() is None to detect 'not found', and catch IntegrityError to report duplicates.

knowledge_points.title: lastrowid: the id of the new row
knowledge_points.worked_example:
cur = db.execute("INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (?)", ("ana",))
print(cur.lastrowid)  # 1
cur = db.execute("INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (?)", ("bo",))
print(cur.lastrowid)  # 2
knowledge_points.practice: Predict lastrowid after a series of inserts; use it to insert a related row.

knowledge_points.title: rowcount 0 means nothing matched
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def delete_user(name):
    cur = db.execute("DELETE FROM users WHERE name = ?", (name,))
    return cur.rowcount > 0
print(delete_user("zed"))  # False: no such user
knowledge_points.practice: Write functions that report whether an update or delete found a row.

knowledge_points.title: Check fetchone() for None before indexing
knowledge_points.worked_example:
row = db.execute("SELECT id FROM users WHERE name = ?", ("zed",)).fetchone()
print(row[0])
# TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not subscriptable
Fix: if row is None: handle 'not found' first.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix lookups that crash when the row is missing.

knowledge_points.title: Catch IntegrityError to report a duplicate
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of add_user calls; choose IntegrityError vs OperationalError for described failures.

topics.title: Creating, changing and removing tables safely
topics.summary: Re-run setup code safely with IF NOT EXISTS, remove tables with DROP TABLE, add a column with ALTER TABLE, and list the tables in a database.

knowledge_points.title: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("CREATE TABLE t2 (x INTEGER)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE t2 (x INTEGER)")
# sqlite3.OperationalError: table t2 already exists
With a file database the second run of your program hits this; IF NOT EXISTS skips the create instead.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix setup code that fails on its second run.

knowledge_points.title: DROP TABLE removes a table and all its rows
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("DROP TABLE IF EXISTS t")
Useful for starting fresh in a script; there is no undo.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose between DELETE FROM t and DROP TABLE t for described goals.

knowledge_points.title: ALTER TABLE adds a column
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("ALTER TABLE t ADD COLUMN y TEXT")
Existing rows get NULL (or the column's DEFAULT) in the new column.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict existing rows after adding a column with and without DEFAULT.

knowledge_points.title: Which tables exist?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(db.execute("SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type = 'table'").fetchall())
# [('t',)]
sqlite_master is SQLite's own table describing the database.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the query that lists tables; predict its output after CREATE and DROP statements.

topics.title: Why one big table goes wrong: splitting data into tables
topics.summary: See the update problems caused by repeating text in every row, move repeated data into its own table referenced by an id, and recognise one-to-many relationships.

knowledge_points.title: Repeated text causes trouble
knowledge_points.worked_example:
track      | artist
Mustapha   | Queen
Bicycle    | Queen
Hello      | Adele
Renaming Queen means updating every Queen row; one typo ('Quen') silently creates a second artist.
knowledge_points.practice: Find the problems (repetition, inconsistent spellings, costly updates) in a flat table.

knowledge_points.title: Move repeated data into its own table
knowledge_points.practice: Split a flat table into two tables; fill in the artist_id values for given rows.

knowledge_points.title: One-to-many: the 'many' side holds the id
knowledge_points.worked_example:
One artist has many tracks; one track has one artist.
So tracks gets an artist_id column, not the other way round: a single artist row cannot hold a list of track ids.
knowledge_points.practice: For pairs of entities (customer/order, author/book), decide the relationship and which table gets the id column.

knowledge_points.title: Model a small domain
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Blog: users write posts; each post has one author.
users (id, name, email UNIQUE)
posts (id, title, body, author_id)
List the things (tables), their facts (columns), then the links (id columns).
knowledge_points.practice: Write the tables for described domains (library loans, a shop's orders).

topics.title: Primary, logical and foreign keys
topics.summary: Name the three kinds of key in a schema, declare foreign keys with REFERENCES, and have SQLite enforce them.

knowledge_points.title: Three kinds of key
knowledge_points.worked_example:
artists (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT UNIQUE)
albums (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title TEXT, artist_id INTEGER)
id: primary key (the row's own number). name: logical key (how people look it up). artist_id: foreign key (points at a row in another table).
knowledge_points.practice: Label the columns of given schemas as primary, logical or foreign key.

knowledge_points.title: Declare a foreign key with REFERENCES
knowledge_points.worked_example:
CREATE TABLE albums (
    id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    title TEXT,
    artist_id INTEGER REFERENCES artists(id))
The declaration documents the link and lets the database check it.
knowledge_points.practice: Write CREATE TABLE statements with REFERENCES for described links.

knowledge_points.title: Turn on checking: PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
... create artists (Queen = 1) and albums ...
db.execute("INSERT INTO albums VALUES ('Ghost', 99)")
# sqlite3.IntegrityError: FOREIGN KEY constraint failed
SQLite only checks foreign keys when this is on; run it right after connecting.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict whether inserts with dangling ids succeed with and without the pragma.

knowledge_points.title: Choose keys that never change
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Using name as the primary key: renaming an artist would break every album pointing at 'Queen'.
An integer id never changes, so links stay valid; keep the name UNIQUE for lookups.
knowledge_points.practice: Pick the best primary key for described tables and justify it.

topics.title: Combining tables with JOIN ... ON
topics.summary: Join two tables by matching a foreign key to a primary key, qualify column names, use table aliases, and recognise the every-combination bug.

knowledge_points.title: JOIN ... ON pairs up matching rows
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT albums.title, artists.name
FROM albums JOIN artists ON albums.artist_id = artists.id
ORDER BY albums.title
# [('25', 'Adele'), ('Innuendo', 'Queen'), ('Jazz', 'Queen')]
(artists: 1 Queen, 2 Adele, 3 Abba; albums Jazz and Innuendo point at 1, 25 at 2.)
knowledge_points.practice: Predict joined rows for two small tables; write the ON condition linking a foreign key to its primary key.

knowledge_points.title: Qualify columns that exist in both tables
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT id, title FROM albums JOIN artists ON albums.artist_id = artists.id
# sqlite3.OperationalError: ambiguous column name: id
Write albums.id or artists.id.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix ambiguous column errors; choose which table's column a query needs.

knowledge_points.title: Aliases and WHERE after the join
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT al.title, ar.name FROM albums AS al
JOIN artists AS ar ON al.artist_id = ar.id
WHERE ar.name = 'Queen'
# [('Jazz', 'Queen'), ('Innuendo', 'Queen')]
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite joins with short aliases; write joins that filter on a column of the other table.

knowledge_points.title: Forgetting ON gives every combination
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM albums JOIN artists   # (9,)
3 albums x 3 artists: every pair, mostly wrong. The older form FROM albums, artists WHERE albums.artist_id = artists.id is the same as a JOIN with ON.
knowledge_points.practice: Compute row counts of joins without ON; fix the query; convert between the comma form and JOIN ... ON.

topics.title: Inserting related rows: look up or create an id
topics.summary: Use INSERT OR IGNORE plus a SELECT to get the id for a name whether or not it exists yet, then insert child rows that point at it.

knowledge_points.title: INSERT OR IGNORE skips duplicates quietly
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO artists (name) VALUES (?)", ("Queen",))
Run twice: one Queen row, no IntegrityError, because name is UNIQUE and the duplicate is ignored.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict table contents after repeated INSERT OR IGNORE; compare with a plain INSERT.

knowledge_points.title: Then SELECT the id
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def artist_id(name):
    db.execute("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO artists (name) VALUES (?)", (name,))
    row = db.execute("SELECT id FROM artists WHERE name = ?", (name,)).fetchone()
    return row[0]
print(artist_id("Queen"), artist_id("Adele"), artist_id("Queen"))  # 1 2 1
knowledge_points.practice: Predict ids returned by a sequence of calls; fill in the missing SELECT.

knowledge_points.title: Insert the child row with the id
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("INSERT INTO albums (title, artist_id) VALUES (?, ?)",
           ("Jazz", artist_id("Queen")))
The parent row is created on first use, so the foreign key always points at a real row.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the insert for a child row; trace both tables after several inserts.

knowledge_points.title: Load flat records into two tables
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for title, artist in [("Jazz", "Queen"), ("25", "Adele"), ("Innuendo", "Queen")]:
    db.execute("INSERT INTO albums (title, artist_id) VALUES (?, ?)",
               (title, artist_id(artist)))
# artists: (1, 'Queen'), (2, 'Adele'); albums point at 1, 2, 1
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the tables built from a list of records; extend the loader to a third level (tracks).

topics.title: Many-to-many relationships: junction tables
topics.summary: Model links where both sides have many partners with a junction table of two foreign keys, a composite primary key, and data stored on the connection.

knowledge_points.title: Recognise many-to-many
knowledge_points.worked_example:
A student takes many courses; a course has many students.
Neither table can hold the link: a course_id column in students would allow only one course per student.
knowledge_points.practice: Classify described relationships as one-to-many or many-to-many.

knowledge_points.title: A junction table holds pairs of ids
knowledge_points.worked_example:
CREATE TABLE enrolments (
    student_id INTEGER REFERENCES students(id),
    course_id INTEGER REFERENCES courses(id))
INSERT INTO enrolments VALUES (1, 1), (1, 2), (2, 1)
Each row is one connection: Ana (1) takes SQL (1) and Art (2).
knowledge_points.practice: Write the junction table for a described pair; fill in its rows from a description.

knowledge_points.title: A composite primary key blocks duplicate links
knowledge_points.worked_example:
PRIMARY KEY (student_id, course_id)
INSERT INTO enrolments VALUES (1, 1, 'teacher')  # again
# sqlite3.IntegrityError: UNIQUE constraint failed: enrolments.student_id, enrolments.course_id
knowledge_points.practice: Predict which inserts into a junction table fail.

knowledge_points.title: Store facts about the connection
knowledge_points.worked_example:
enrolments (student_id, course_id, role)
(1, 1, 'student'), (1, 2, 'teacher')
A role belongs to the pair, not to the student or the course alone.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide where described facts belong (student, course or enrolment).

topics.title: Keeping rows without a match: LEFT JOIN
topics.summary: Use LEFT JOIN to keep rows that have no partner, find those rows with IS NULL, and count correctly with COUNT(column).

knowledge_points.title: JOIN drops rows without a partner; LEFT JOIN keeps them
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT artists.name, albums.title FROM artists
LEFT JOIN albums ON albums.artist_id = artists.id ORDER BY artists.name
# [('Abba', None), ('Adele', '25'), ('Queen', 'Innuendo'), ('Queen', 'Jazz')]
Abba has no albums: an inner JOIN would leave Abba out.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the rows of JOIN vs LEFT JOIN for the same tables.

knowledge_points.title: Find rows with no match
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT artists.name FROM artists
LEFT JOIN albums ON albums.artist_id = artists.id
WHERE albums.id IS NULL
# [('Abba',)]
knowledge_points.practice: Write queries for 'customers with no orders', 'books never borrowed'.

knowledge_points.title: Count with COUNT(column), not COUNT(*)
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT artists.name, COUNT(albums.id) FROM artists
LEFT JOIN albums ON albums.artist_id = artists.id GROUP BY artists.name
# Abba 0, Adele 1, Queen 2
COUNT(*) would give Abba 1, counting the row of NULLs.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix per-group counts that report 1 instead of 0.

knowledge_points.title: Which table goes on the left matters
knowledge_points.worked_example:
artists LEFT JOIN albums keeps every artist.
albums LEFT JOIN artists keeps every album (and drops Abba).
The table whose rows you must keep goes first.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose the table order for described questions.

topics.title: Joining three tables and many-to-many data
topics.summary: Chain joins across three tables, including through a junction table, and filter and aggregate the joined rows.

knowledge_points.title: Chain one-to-many joins
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT tracks.title, albums.title, artists.name
FROM tracks
JOIN albums ON tracks.album_id = albums.id
JOIN artists ON albums.artist_id = artists.id
ORDER BY tracks.title
# [('Bicycle Race', 'Jazz', 'Queen'), ('Hello', '25', 'Adele'), ('Mustapha', 'Jazz', 'Queen')]
knowledge_points.practice: Write the second JOIN for a three-table chain; predict joined rows.

knowledge_points.title: Join through a junction table
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT students.name, courses.title, enrolments.role
FROM enrolments
JOIN students ON enrolments.student_id = students.id
JOIN courses ON enrolments.course_id = courses.id
ORDER BY students.name, courses.title
# [('Ana', 'Art', 'teacher'), ('Ana', 'SQL', 'student'), ('Bo', 'SQL', 'student')]
knowledge_points.practice: Order the lines of a junction-table join (Parsons); predict its rows.

knowledge_points.title: Filter the joined rows
knowledge_points.worked_example:
... same joins ...
WHERE students.name = 'Ana' AND enrolments.role = 'student'
# [('Ana', 'SQL', 'student')]
knowledge_points.practice: Write joins that answer 'which courses does X teach'.

knowledge_points.title: Aggregate across a join
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT courses.title, COUNT(*) FROM enrolments
JOIN courses ON enrolments.course_id = courses.id
GROUP BY courses.title ORDER BY courses.title
# [('Art', 1), ('SQL', 2)]
knowledge_points.practice: Write per-group counts over joined data; predict results.

topics.title: Queries inside queries: subqueries
topics.summary: Use a subquery's result as a value or a list inside WHERE, and recognise when a join gives the same answer.

knowledge_points.title: Compare with a computed value
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT title, year FROM books WHERE year < (SELECT AVG(year) FROM books)
# [('Emma', 1815), ('Persuasion', 1817)]
The inner query runs first and becomes one number.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of single-value subqueries; write 'above average' queries.

knowledge_points.title: Find the row holding the maximum
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT title FROM books WHERE price = (SELECT MAX(price) FROM books)
# [('Dune',)]
SELECT title, MAX(price) alone does not tell you which rows tie for it.
knowledge_points.practice: Write queries for the most expensive / oldest item.

knowledge_points.title: IN with a list from another table
knowledge_points.worked_example:
SELECT name FROM students
WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrolments WHERE role = 'teacher')
# [('Ana',)]
knowledge_points.practice: Predict results of IN-subqueries; write one for a described question.

knowledge_points.title: Subquery or join?
knowledge_points.worked_example:
The IN query above gives the same names as
SELECT DISTINCT students.name FROM students JOIN enrolments ON ... WHERE role = 'teacher'
Use a join when you also need columns from the other table.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose between a subquery and a join for given questions; rewrite one as the other.

topics.title: Rows you can read by column name: sqlite3.Row
topics.summary: Set row_factory to sqlite3.Row to read columns by name, convert rows to dictionaries, and turn query results into JSON-ready lists of dicts.

knowledge_points.title: row['title'] instead of row[0]
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
row = db.execute("SELECT * FROM books").fetchone()
print(row["title"], row[1])  # Dune 1965
Set row_factory once, right after connecting; index numbers still work.
knowledge_points.practice: Rewrite index-based row access with column names; predict printed values.

knowledge_points.title: dict(row) and row.keys()
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(dict(row))    # {'title': 'Dune', 'year': 1965}
print(row.keys())   # ['title', 'year']
knowledge_points.practice: Predict dict(row) for queries selecting different columns.

knowledge_points.title: A query result as a list of dicts, then JSON
knowledge_points.worked_example:
books = [dict(r) for r in db.execute("SELECT * FROM books")]
print(json.dumps(books))  # [{"title": "Dune", "year": 1965}]
This is the shape a web API sends back.
knowledge_points.practice: Write the comprehension that converts a query to a list of dicts; predict the JSON text.

knowledge_points.title: Unknown column names raise IndexError
knowledge_points.worked_example:
print(row["Title"])   # Dune: names ignore case
print(row["author"])
# IndexError: No item with that key
knowledge_points.practice: Fix lookups of columns the query did not select.

topics.title: From a file to a database: loading and reporting
topics.summary: Read records from a CSV or text file, convert and insert them, then answer questions with SQL instead of Python loops (the py4e counting pattern).

knowledge_points.title: Read CSV rows and insert them
knowledge_points.worked_example:
with open("sales.csv") as f:
    reader = csv.reader(f)
    next(reader)                       # skip the header
    rows = []
    for item, city, amount in reader:
        rows.append((item, city, int(amount)))
db.executemany("INSERT INTO sales VALUES (?, ?, ?)", rows)
knowledge_points.practice: Order the lines of a loader (Parsons); fill in the executemany call.

knowledge_points.title: Convert types before inserting
knowledge_points.worked_example:
db.execute("CREATE TABLE s (amount TEXT)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO s VALUES ('10'), ('9')")
print(db.execute("SELECT MAX(amount) FROM s").fetchone())  # ('9',)
csv gives strings; stored as text, '9' beats '10'. Convert with int() and use INTEGER columns.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict MAX/ORDER BY on text vs numbers; fix a loader that stores numbers as text.

knowledge_points.title: Let SQL write the report
knowledge_points.worked_example:
for city, total in db.execute("SELECT city, SUM(amount) FROM sales GROUP BY city ORDER BY city"):
    print(f"{city}: {total}")
# Oslo: 5
# Paris: 5
knowledge_points.practice: Write the query and print loop for a requested report.

knowledge_points.title: Count as you read: update or insert
knowledge_points.practice: Trace the counts table over a short mailbox; place db.commit() correctly.

topics.title: How a web app works: requests, routes and responses
topics.summary: Describe what happens between a browser and a Python web server, and model routing as a dictionary that maps paths to functions returning a body and a status code.

knowledge_points.title: The server side of the request-response cycle
knowledge_points.worked_example:
1. The browser sends GET /about (a request like the ones in HTTP basics)
2. The server finds the Python function for the path /about
3. The function builds the page
4. The server sends a response: status code, headers and HTML
5. The browser draws the HTML
As a client you read requests and responses; a web app is the program on the other end that produces them.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the steps of a request (Parsons); say which steps run on the server.

knowledge_points.title: Routing: the path picks a function
knowledge_points.practice: Add a route to the table; predict what a path returns.

knowledge_points.title: Unknown paths get 404
knowledge_points.practice: Predict handle() results; choose the status code your server should send for described situations.

knowledge_points.title: Front end, back end, database
knowledge_points.worked_example:
Front end: HTML/CSS/JavaScript the browser shows.
Back end: Python code that handles requests.
Database: where the back end keeps data between requests.
A static page is a fixed file; a dynamic page is built per request.
knowledge_points.practice: Assign described jobs to front end, back end or database; classify pages as static or dynamic.

topics.title: Just enough HTML to build pages from Python
topics.summary: Write the handful of HTML tags a Python web app needs (headings, paragraphs, links, lists, forms), build HTML strings in Python, and escape user text.

knowledge_points.title: Tags, nesting and attributes
knowledge_points.worked_example:
My books

Read about me.

A tag opens

and closes

; tags nest; attributes like href="/about" go in the opening tag.
knowledge_points.practice: Fix mis-nested or unclosed tags; write the HTML for a described snippet.

knowledge_points.title: Build HTML in Python
knowledge_points.worked_example:
books = ["Dune", "Emma"] items = "" for b in books: items += f"
  • {b}
    • " print(f"
      {items}
    ") #
    • Dune
    • Emma
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the HTML a loop builds; write code that builds a list or table from data.

knowledge_points.title: Forms send named fields
knowledge_points.worked_example:
<form action="/add" method="post">
  <input name="title">
  <button>Add</button>
</form>
Submitting sends title=<what was typed> to /add; the server reads it by the name 'title'.
knowledge_points.practice: Read a form and say which path receives it, with which method and field names; fix a form whose input lacks a name.

knowledge_points.title: Escape user text before putting it in HTML
knowledge_points.worked_example:
import html name = "" print(f"

Hello {html.escape(name)}

") #

Hello <script>alert('hi')</script>

Unescaped, the browser would run the script: an XSS attack.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict escaped output; spot the line that puts unescaped user input into a page.

topics.title: A first Flask app: routes and the development server
topics.summary: Install Flask, write an app with @app.route view functions, run the development server in debug mode, and test pages without a browser using the test client.

knowledge_points.title: Hello, Flask
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from flask import Flask app = Flask(__name__) @app.route("/") def home(): return "

Hello

" $ flask --app hello run # Running on http://127.0.0.1:5000 (python3 -m pip install flask first.) The decorator registers home() for the path /.
knowledge_points.practice: Order the lines of a minimal app (Parsons); say which URL shows which text.

knowledge_points.title: More pages, more routes
knowledge_points.practice: Add routes for described pages; predict the response for listed paths.

knowledge_points.title: Test a page with the test client
knowledge_points.worked_example:
client = app.test_client() r = client.get("/about") print(r.status_code) # 200 print(r.get_data(as_text=True)) #

About me

No server or browser needed, so pages can be checked like any function.
knowledge_points.practice: Write test-client checks for a route's status and text; predict status codes for missing routes.

knowledge_points.title: Debug mode: reload and tracebacks
knowledge_points.worked_example:
$ flask --app hello run --debug
The server restarts when you save, and an exception in a view shows a traceback page instead of 500 Internal Server Error. Never turn debug on for a public site.
knowledge_points.practice: Match symptoms (stale page, 500 error) to causes; choose when debug mode is safe.

topics.title: Routes with variables: <name> and <int:id>
topics.summary: Capture parts of the URL as view-function arguments, convert them with int:, and avoid duplicate view names.

knowledge_points.title: <name> becomes an argument
knowledge_points.practice: Predict responses for URLs; write a route with one variable.

knowledge_points.title: <int:n> converts and rejects
knowledge_points.practice: Fix views that do arithmetic on a string variable; predict responses for valid and invalid URLs.

knowledge_points.title: Several variables; unique view names
knowledge_points.practice: Write routes with two variables; fix duplicate view names.

knowledge_points.title: A URL game
knowledge_points.practice: Predict pages for a list of URLs; extend the game with a new response.

topics.title: HTML templates, static files and url_for
topics.summary: Keep HTML in a templates folder and render it with render_template, pass values into it, serve CSS and images from static, and build links with url_for.

knowledge_points.title: render_template reads templates/
knowledge_points.worked_example:
project/
  app.py
  templates/index.html
return render_template("index.html")
The file must be inside templates/, or Flask raises jinja2.exceptions.TemplateNotFound: index.html
knowledge_points.practice: Arrange files so a template is found; fix a TemplateNotFound error.

knowledge_points.title: Pass values to the template
knowledge_points.worked_example:
return render_template("hello.html", name=name, year=2026)

Hi {{ name }}

{{ year }}
Each keyword argument becomes a name the template can use; Jinja syntax is the next concept.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict rendered HTML; add the missing keyword argument.

knowledge_points.title: Static files: CSS and images
knowledge_points.worked_example:
static/style.css
<link rel="stylesheet" href="{{ url_for('static', filename='style.css') }}">
Files in static/ are served as they are, at /static/<filename>.
knowledge_points.practice: Choose templates/ or static/ for given files; write the url_for for an image.

knowledge_points.title: url_for builds links from view names
knowledge_points.worked_example: url_for("hello", name="ana") # '/hello/ana' Say hi If the route's path changes, links built with url_for still work.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the URLs url_for builds; replace hard-coded links.

topics.title: Handling forms: POST requests, request.form and redirects
topics.summary: Accept GET and POST on one route, read submitted fields from request.form and query strings from request.args, and redirect after a successful POST.

knowledge_points.title: One route, two methods
knowledge_points.practice: Predict responses to GET and POST; fix a route that rejects POST.

knowledge_points.title: Read fields with request.form
knowledge_points.worked_example:
title = request.form["title"]
notes = request.form.get("notes", "")
client.post("/add", data={"title": "Dune"})   # test it
A missing key in request.form[...] gives 400 Bad Request; .get() returns a default.
knowledge_points.practice: Match form field names to request.form keys; choose [ ] or .get() for required and optional fields.

knowledge_points.title: Query strings with request.args
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# GET /search?q=dune
q = request.args.get("q", "")
Search forms use method="get", so their fields arrive in the URL and in request.args.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict request.args values for URLs; choose GET or POST for described forms.

knowledge_points.title: Redirect after POST
knowledge_points.practice: Fix views that render after POST; predict the status code (302) of a redirect.

topics.title: Status codes, error pages and flash messages
topics.summary: Return a chosen status code, stop with abort(404), show a custom error page, and give one-time feedback with flash messages.

knowledge_points.title: Return a status code with the body
knowledge_points.practice: Predict status codes for requests; add a status to a view.

knowledge_points.title: abort() and custom error pages
knowledge_points.practice: Choose abort(404) vs abort(403) vs abort(400) for situations; fix an error handler that forgets the status.

knowledge_points.title: flash() for one-time messages
knowledge_points.practice: Order the steps of a save-then-flash flow; predict on which page a message appears.

topics.title: Jinja templates: {{ expressions }}, filters and escaping
topics.summary: Insert values, dictionary keys and attributes into a template, transform them with filters, and know when Jinja escapes HTML for you.

knowledge_points.title: {{ }} prints an expression
knowledge_points.worked_example:
from jinja2 import Template
print(Template("Hi {{ name }}, total {{ price * 2 }}").render(name="Ana", price=3))
# Hi Ana, total 6
Flask's render_template does the same with a file.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict rendered text for templates with variables and arithmetic.

knowledge_points.title: Keys and attributes: post.title
knowledge_points.worked_example:
render_template("post.html", post={"title": "Hi", "body": "..."})

{{ post.title }}

(same as {{ post['title'] }}) The dot works for dictionary keys and object attributes alike.
knowledge_points.practice: Write template expressions for nested data; predict output.

knowledge_points.title: Filters transform values
knowledge_points.worked_example:
{{ name | upper }}         ANA
{{ posts | length }}       3
{{ price | round(2) }}     9.5
{{ nick | default('anon') }}
A filter takes the value on its left, like a function call.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict filter results; choose the filter for a described display.

knowledge_points.title: Escaping, |safe and silent typos
knowledge_points.worked_example: In Flask's .html templates, {{ comment }} with 'hi' shows <b>hi</b>: user text cannot inject HTML. {{ post.body | safe }} turns escaping off, only for HTML you trust. {{ nmae }} (typo) renders as nothing, with no error.
knowledge_points.practice: Decide where |safe is acceptable; find the typo behind a blank spot on a page.

topics.title: Jinja loops and conditions: {% for %} and {% if %}
topics.summary: Generate repeated HTML with {% for %}, choose content with {% if %}, use loop variables and an empty-list else, and link each item to its own page.

knowledge_points.title: {% for %} repeats HTML
knowledge_points.worked_example:
{% for post in posts %}
  • {{ post.title }}
    • {% endfor %}
Every {% for %} needs {% endfor %}; indentation does not matter in templates.
knowledge_points.practice: Predict the HTML for a list of dicts; fix a template missing endfor.

knowledge_points.title: {% if %} chooses content
knowledge_points.practice: Predict rendered output for different values; write an if/elif block.

knowledge_points.title: loop.index and an else for empty lists
knowledge_points.practice: Predict numbered output and the empty case.

knowledge_points.title: A link per item
knowledge_points.practice: Write the loop that links each item; predict the hrefs generated.

topics.title: Sharing a layout: {% extends %}, {% block %} and {% include %}
topics.summary: Put the shared page layout in a base template, fill its blocks from child templates, and reuse snippets with include.

knowledge_points.title: A base template with blocks

import hashlib

# f52fbd32b2b3b86ff88ef6c490628285f482af15ddcb29541f94bcf526a3f6c7

knowledge_points.title: register(): hash, then insert
knowledge_points.worked_example:
# hash_pw(pw, salt) as in the previous topic (pbkdf2 version)
def register(username, pw):
    salt = secrets.token_hex(8)
    try:
        db.execute("INSERT INTO users (username, salt, pw_hash) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
                   (username, salt, hash_pw(pw, salt)))
        return True
    except sqlite3.IntegrityError:   # username is UNIQUE
        return False
print(register("ana", "correct horse"), register("ana", "other"))  # True False
knowledge_points.practice: Order the lines of register (Parsons); predict results of repeated registrations.

knowledge_points.title: login(): look up, then compare
knowledge_points.worked_example:
def login(username, pw):
    row = db.execute("SELECT salt, pw_hash FROM users WHERE username = ?", (username,)).fetchone()
    if row is None:
        return False
    salt, stored = row
    return hash_pw(pw, salt) == stored
print(login("ana", "correct horse"), login("ana", "wrong"), login("zed", "x"))  # True False False
knowledge_points.practice: Predict login results; fix a login that crashes for unknown users.
